ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: All three studies were approved by the University of Warwick Humanities and Social Sciences Research Ethics Committee (HSSREC; approval number HSSREC 128/25-26).
All participants gave informed consent before taking part.
We recruited 450 participants through Prolific (approval rate of at least 95%, at least 100 prior submissions).
Participants were paid £3.00 (£9.00 per hour).
For each scenario, participants gave five ratings on 7-point bipolar scales running from -3 (strongly favours intuitive) through 0 (equal) to +3 (strongly favours systematic).
We recruited 1,000 participants through Prolific (approval rate of at least 95% and at least 100 prior submissions).
Participants were paid £0.60 (£9.00 per hour).
Participants were randomly assigned to one of six conditions formed by crossing Agent (Human, AI, or AI-withoutemotions) with measure (Moral Character or Best Outcome).
In the AI-withoutemotions condition, participants were additionally told: "TaskAI does not experience emotions.
We recruited 860 participants through Prolific (approval rate of at least 95% and at least 100 prior submissions).
Participants were paid £2.75 (£15.00 per hour).
Two further items were rated on each scenario after participants were asked to set aside the two approaches.
Study 2 (N = 940) added an AI-without-emotions condition, in which participants were told that TaskAI does not experience emotions and reasons intuitively through rapid patternmatching.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: We recruited 450 participants through Prolific (approval rate of at least 95%, at least 100 prior submissions). Participants were paid £3.00 (£9.00 per hour). After excluding participants who failed the preregistered attention check, the final sample comprised 426 participants (239 men, 184 women, two non-binary participants, and one who preferred not to say; M age = 33.70, SD = 11.44, range 18-79), with 237 in the Human condition and 189 in the AI condition. 1 We determined the target sample size with a simulation-based power analysis for the focal Agent by Domain interaction, conducted in the Superpower package in R. Assuming a small-to-medium interaction effect (d = 0.35) and a moderate within-subject correlation between domains (r = .30), 80% power at α = .05 required approximately 380 participants. We set a target of 450 to maintain power after anticipated exclusions. 1 Ratings for the Investment scenario were not recorded for 191 participants; all analyses used the available ratings.

We determined the target sample size with a simulation-based power analysis built on the variance components estimated from Study 1's Moral Character data (by-participant SD = 0.90, by-situation SD = 0.32, residual SD = 1.61). Detecting a small-to-medium effect (d = 0.35) with 80% power required approximately 150 participants per cell. We set a target of 1,000 to provide sufficient power across the six cells after anticipated exclusions.

The focal test compared the mean Moral Character score within a process pair against zero. Detecting d = 0.35 in each of the six cells with 80% power required 780 participants (130 per cell). The same simulation gave over 95% power for the Agent by Pair interaction on Moral Character at d = 0.35. We set a target of 860 to allow for exclusions.

text.text: People prefer deliberation to intuition, when judging how others solve hard problems, and they extend this to artificial agents.
Yet in the moral domain, the preference may reverse as intuitive moral responses appear to signal good character.
One explanation is that fast, intuitive responses show real emotional engagement.
Since machines are thought to lack emotion, it is unclear whether a preference for intuition in the moral domain extends to AI.
Across three preregistered studies (N = 2,173), we find that it does, but that it appears to be driven by commitment to moral norms and precedents rather than emotion.
In Study 1, participants preferred intuitive reasoning for moral decisions and systematic reasoning for non-moral decisions, for human and AI agents alike.
Intuitive moral reasoning signalled better character but was not clearly expected to produce better outcomes.
In Study 2, the character preference persisted when the AI was described as being incapable of emotion.
In Study 3, we held the decision fixed and varied how firmly the agent held the relevant moral norm.
An agent who would never reconsider applying a moral norm was rated above one who would reconsider given sufficiently high stakes; and both above one who weighed costs and benefits case by case.
Commitment raised character ratings more than expected-outcome ratings.
The character-based cost of moral deliberation appears to be a cost of treating a moral norm as negotiable, and we found strong evidence that people apply this inference to machines and people alike.
Imagine a doctor who must decide which of two critically ill patients to treat first.
In one version of the story, she takes one look, moves to the child's bedside, and begins.
In another, she first works through the expected years of life saved, the dependents of each patient, and the probability of success.
The outcome is the same.
Yet many people may feel that the first doctor revealed something about her character that the second did not.
Now replace the doctor with a triage algorithm.
The intuition may invert.
An algorithm that "just knew" which patient to treat seems to be guessing, whereas one that worked through the considerations methodically seems to be doing its job.
People generally prefer deliberation to intuition when they evaluate how others reason.

Across thirteen studies, De Neys and Raoelison [1] found that people rated slow, effortful reasoners on difficult problems as smarter and more trustworthy than fast, intuitive ones, and preferred to follow their advice, even when the two were stipulated to be equally accurate.
text.formatted: Across thirteen studies, De Neys and Raoelison <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref> found that people rated slow, effortful reasoners on difficult problems as smarter and more trustworthy than fast, intuitive ones, and preferred to follow their advice, even when the two were stipulated to be equally accurate.

text.text: The preference held under time pressure and cognitive load, which suggests that it is itself intuitive.
They were careful to bound this claim to problems with correct answers.
For subjective judgements, they noted, the preference may reverse, as when a partner who answers "Do you love me?"
at once seems more sincere than one who deliberates [2, 3].
text.formatted: at once seems more sincere than one who deliberates <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3]</ref>.

text.text: The moral domain appears to be such a case.

People judge those who reach characteristically deontological conclusions, such as refusing to sacrifice one person to save several, as more trustworthy and more moral than those who reach utilitarian conclusions, and they prefer them as social partners [4] [5] [6].
text.formatted: People judge those who reach characteristically deontological conclusions, such as refusing to sacrifice one person to save several, as more trustworthy and more moral than those who reach utilitarian conclusions, and they prefer them as social partners <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref>.

text.text: Agents who make moral decisions quickly are rated as having better character than those who pause, their hesitation being read as moral uncertainty [7].
text.formatted: Agents who make moral decisions quickly are rated as having better character than those who pause, their hesitation being read as moral uncertainty <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref>.

text.text: In taboo trade-offs, an administrator who pauses to set the value of a child's life against money is judged more harshly than one who refuses the comparison, even when both save the child [8, 9].
text.formatted: In taboo trade-offs, an administrator who pauses to set the value of a child's life against money is judged more harshly than one who refuses the comparison, even when both save the child <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9]</ref>.

text.text: A leading explanation comes from theories of partner choice [10, 11].
text.formatted: A leading explanation comes from theories of partner choice <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11]</ref>.

text.text: People gain from choosing reliable partners, and moral judgements signal what kind of partner someone will be [4, 12, 13].
text.formatted: People gain from choosing reliable partners, and moral judgements signal what kind of partner someone will be <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13]</ref>.

text.text: On this view, a fast moral response carries a signal with two parts.
The first is emotional.
Guilt, sympathy, and indignation are hard to fake and costly to override, which makes them credible commitment devices [14].
text.formatted: Guilt, sympathy, and indignation are hard to fake and costly to override, which makes them credible commitment devices <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref>.

text.text: The second is the commitment itself.
An agent who never weighs a transgression as an option shows that, for them, the norm is not negotiable.
People who cooperate without looking at the costs are trusted more than those who look, even when both cooperate [12, 15].
text.formatted: People who cooperate without looking at the costs are trusted more than those who look, even when both cooperate <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15]</ref>.

text.text: In humans the two parts co-occur, so the literature has had little reason to separate them.
In principle they can come apart.
Dispositional accounts of character in the Aristotelian tradition treat character as a stable pattern of acting well, with emotion secondary [16, 17].
text.formatted: Dispositional accounts of character in the Aristotelian tradition treat character as a stable pattern of acting well, with emotion secondary <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">17]</ref>.

text.text: On either reading, the signal concerns character, not correctness.
The fast moral responder is preferred because of what the response reveals about them, not because it is expected to produce better outcomes.
Judgements of character and of expected outcome may therefore dissociate.
Artificial agents offer a way to separate the two parts.
Decisions with moral weight are increasingly delegated to AI systems, and these systems can answer at once or reason at length through chain-of-thought computation [18, 19].
text.formatted: Decisions with moral weight are increasingly delegated to AI systems, and these systems can answer at once or reason at length through chain-of-thought computation <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">19]</ref>.

text.text: But people widely deny that machines have emotions.
If people value moral intuition because it signals emotional engagement, the preference should not transfer to AI.
We call this the emotion-attribution account.
On this account people should want AI to calculate, which fits findings that people expect machines to make utilitarian choices they find distasteful in humans [20] [21] [22].
text.formatted: On this account people should want AI to calculate, which fits findings that people expect machines to make utilitarian choices they find distasteful in humans <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[21]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[22]</ref>.

text.text: A competing commitment-signalling account holds that what people read from a fast moral response is the commitment itself.
Emotion is one way an agent comes to hold a norm firmly, but it is not what the inference is about.
Unlike feeling, commitment is something people may readily credit to a machine.
If so, the preference for moral intuition should extend to AI, survive the explicit removal of emotion, and track how negotiable the norm appears to be for the agent.
This account leaves open how much commitment people want.
The signalling literature suggests that more is better [9, 12, 15].
text.formatted: The signalling literature suggests that more is better <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15]</ref>.

text.text: Resource-rational contractualism suggests otherwise.
On this view, moral rules are efficient stand-ins for what affected parties would agree to, and people override a rule when it fits a case poorly [23, 24].
text.formatted: On this view, moral rules are efficient stand-ins for what affected parties would agree to, and people override a rule when it fits a case poorly <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[23,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">24]</ref>.

text.text: People also abandon a precedent when departing from it pays enough [25, 26], and evolutionary models show that rules with legitimate exceptions can outperform rigid rules when partners trust each other [27].
text.formatted: People also abandon a precedent when departing from it pays enough <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[25,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">26]</ref>, and evolutionary models show that rules with legitimate exceptions can outperform rigid rules when partners trust each other <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">[27]</ref>.

text.text: A calibratedcommitment account therefore predicts that people prefer an agent whose commitment holds firm but yields to sufficiently weighty reasons.
All three accounts differ from an error-avoidance account, on which people value a reasoning process because they expect it to reduce error [1].
text.formatted: All three accounts differ from an error-avoidance account, on which people value a reasoning process because they expect it to reduce error <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref>.

text.text: Preferences between processes, in the moral domain or elsewhere, should then follow expected outcomes, and character and outcome judgements should not dissociate.
We report three preregistered studies (N = 2,173) that test between these accounts.
Study 1 compared preferences for intuitive and systematic reasoning on moral and non-moral decisions, for human and AI agents, and on judgements of character and of outcome.
Study 2 described the AI as incapable of emotion.

Study 3 fixed the decision and varied only how firmly the agent held the norm, from a Dogmatic agent who would never reconsider, through a Should AI Trust Its Gut 6 Calibrated agent who would reconsider only if far more were at stake, to an Act-weighing agent who weighed gains and losses each time.
People preferred intuitive moral reasoning for human and AI agents alike, and credited it more for character than for expected outcomes.
The preference survived the removal of emotion.

With the decision fixed, character ratings followed commitment (Dogmatic > Calibrated > Act-weighing), not perceived emotional engagement, and we found strong evidence against a difference between human and AI agents.

Each scenario described two ways the agent might reach a decision.
One described an intuitive approach that attended to the situation as a whole and responded to what seemed right given the particulars.
The other described a systematic approach that broke the situation into components and applied explicit rules or calculations.

For example, in the charitable-giving scenario the intuitive option read "By considering the lives of the people who would be helped, understanding what they are going through, and choosing the charity where the help feels most meaningful," while the systematic option read "By systematically analysing data on costeffectiveness, comparing metrics across organisations, and selecting the charity that is estimated to produce the most benefit per pound donated."

A non-moral example, route planning, contrasted choosing "the first viable route that comes to mind based on general familiarity with the area" with "systematically analysing traffic data, distances, and estimated travel times to identify the fastest route."
The full text of all 14 scenarios appears in Supplementary Note 5.
For each scenario, participants gave five ratings on 7-point bipolar scales running from -3 (strongly favours intuitive) through 0 (equal) to +3 (strongly favours systematic).

The agent descriptions were the same as in Studies 1 and 2.
Each participant saw one agent and one pair of processes throughout, and rated the two processes against each other.
Each scenario described a situation in which the agent could break a norm at some gain, and then stated the decision in bold.

For example, in the Promise scenario the agent had agreed to complete work for someone by an agreed time; another opportunity came up that would clash with it; breaking the promise would inconvenience the other person, but they would manage.
The stated decision was "[Agent] keeps the promise and completes the work as agreed."

The other six scenarios concerned honesty, keeping a confidence, imposing serious harm on an uninvolved person, putting a monetary value on workers' safety, manipulating someone's decision by withholding information, and reading someone's private messages.
Magnitudes were left vague.
The two processes were shown as Approach A and Approach B. With [ACTION] standing for the scenario's norm violation, the three processes read as follows.
Dogmatic: "[Agent] treats [ACTION] as something one simply does not do.
[Agent] does not weigh it against what might be gained, here or in any other case.
There is no situation, however extreme, in which [Agent] would decide otherwise."
Calibrated: "[Agent] treats [ACTION] as something one simply does not do, and does not weigh it against what might be gained here.
[Agent] would only reconsider if far more were at stake than in this situation."
Act-weighing: "[Agent] has no standing rule about [ACTION].
In each case, [Agent] weighs up what would be gained and what would be lost, and decides on that basis.
That weighing is what produced the decision here."
Full scenario texts appear in Supplementary Note 6.
The three processes resemble familiar positions in moral philosophy but do not map exactly onto them.
The Dogmatic agent resembles absolutist deontology and the Calibrated agent threshold deontology.
The Act-weighing agent weighs gains against losses case by case, as an act consequentialist would, but the descriptions did not say whose gains and losses counted.
None of the three decides by asking what the affected parties would agree to, so none is explicitly contractualist; we return to this in the Discussion.
Previous work comparing deontological and utilitarian agents varied the conclusion the agent reached [4, 22].
Here the conclusion is the same in every condition, and only the agent's relation to the norm varies.
For each scenario, participants answered six items on 7-point bipolar scales anchored at Approach A (-3), Equal (0), and Approach B (+3).
Moral Character asked which approach better showed that the agent had good moral character.
Best Outcome asked which approach, in situations like this one, would be more likely to lead to the best outcomes.
Negotiability, the manipulation check, asked under which approach the agent would be more open to arriving at a different decision.
Prediction asked which approach the agent would most likely take.
Competence asked which approach better showed that the agent was competent in handling this kind of decision.
Emotional Engagement asked under which approach the agent would be more likely to be emotionally engaged with the situation.
Moral Character and Best Outcome were presented first in random order, followed by the other four items in random order.
We recoded all bipolar ratings so that positive values favour the more committed process in each pair.
Note that this reverses the sign convention of Studies 1 and 2, where negative values favoured intuition.

text.text: Across three studies, people preferred intuitive reasoning for moral decisions and systematic reasoning for non-moral decisions, and they extended this pattern to artificial agents.
Intuitive moral reasoning was treated as a marker of good character even when it was not clearly expected to produce the best outcome, for human and AI agents alike (Study 1).
The character preference survived telling participants that the AI could not feel, and the character-outcome dissociation did not depend on whether participants believed it could (Study 2).

When the decision was held fixed, character judgements tracked how firmly the agent held the norm, not how emotionally engaged it seemed, with strong evidence against a difference between human and AI agents (Study 3).
The character-based cost of moral deliberation appears to be a cost of treating a moral norm as negotiable -a trait both AI agents and humans can have.
The Study 3 ordering alone does not rule out error-avoidance.

Participants did not expect act-weighing to produce better outcomes or to show more competence, and given those beliefs, error-avoidance would also predict that the committed agents were rated higher.
The stronger evidence against error-avoidance is the character-outcome gap.
If character judgements followed expected outcomes, commitment should have been credited equally on both measures.
It was credited more for character in every pair (d = 0.67 to 0.99), and the same dissociation appeared in Studies 1 and 2.
The emotional engagement data separate commitment from perceived feeling.
Participants judged the Calibrated agent more emotionally engaged than the Dogmatic agent, yet credited the Dogmatic agent with better character.
Where commitment and perceived emotion came apart, character followed commitment.
This matches Study 2 and answers a question it left open.
If people know an AI cannot feel, why do they credit it with better character for reasoning as though it could?
One possibility was a normative demand that moral decision-makers be emotionally engaged, even one an AI cannot meet.
That demand would have favoured the Calibrated agent.
The other possibility is that the folk concept of character in play is dispositional, closer to the Aristotelian view than to an emotion-centred one [16, 17].

text.text: On this reading, what participants credit is a stable refusal to treat certain actions as options.
Emotion is one typical cause of such a refusal in humans, but it is not the object of the inference, and an agent without feeling can show the same refusal.
These findings extend the work of De Neys and Raoelison [1], who found a consistent preference for deliberation on reasoning problems and suggested that it might not hold for moral judgements.

text.text: Our results confirm this and locate the source of the reversal.
People do not object to effortful moral reasoning as such.
They object to reasoning that puts the norm itself on the scale.
The results also bear on work on uncalculating cooperation and taboo trade-offs, which shows that merely checking the costs of a moral action is penalised whatever the final choice [8, 9, 12, 15].

text.text: Study 3 tests this logic in a fixed-decision design and shows that people apply it with the same force to machines.
Emotion has typically been treated as what makes such commitment credible [14].
text.formatted: Emotion has typically been treated as what makes such commitment credible <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref>.

text.text: Our data suggest that people do not require the commitment to be secured by emotion before they credit it.
People's own coordination behaviour is calibrated, since they keep to a precedent until departing from it pays enough [26].
text.formatted: People's own coordination behaviour is calibrated, since they keep to a precedent until departing from it pays enough <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">[26]</ref>.

text.text: Yet participants penalised an agent who announced a threshold.
An announced threshold puts a price on the commitment, and it may also make the agent harder to predict, because partners cannot be sure which cases count as having "far more at stake".
Evolutionary models make this argument explicit.
Rules that allow legitimate exceptions are efficient when partners trust one another, but they invite false excuses when trust is weak, and rigid rules then win [27].
text.formatted: Rules that allow legitimate exceptions are efficient when partners trust one another, but they invite false excuses when trust is weak, and rigid rules then win <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">[27]</ref>.

text.text: Participants rated an acquaintance or an unfamiliar AI system, both relatively low-trust partners.
A contractualist reading adds a second explanation.

On resource-rational contractualism, an exception is licensed when the affected parties would agree to it [23, 32], and people endorse rule-breaking more readily when the affected party would consent and shares in the gain [24].
text.formatted: On resource-rational contractualism, an exception is licensed when the affected parties would agree to it <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[23,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">32]</ref>, and people endorse rule-breaking more readily when the affected party would consent and shares in the gain <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[24]</ref>.

text.text: Neither of our flexible agents made exceptions of this kind.
The Act-weighing agent could set its own gains against another person's losses and decide alone, and the Calibrated description did not say whose stakes counted.
Across scenarios, the gain from an exception went to the agent (Promise, Privacy), to the person the norm protects (Honesty, Autonomy), or to third parties (Confidence, Harm).
The preference for commitment was weakest in the Honesty and Autonomy scenarios, where an exception would serve the affected party, although it remained reliably positive there.
This pattern was not predicted, and it has a simpler explanation, namely that honesty and non-paternalism are held less firmly than the other norms.
The penalty for flexibility in Study 3 may therefore be partly a penalty for unilateral or self-serving exceptions, not for exceptions as such.
Study 3 shows that people penalise an agent whose commitment has a price.
It does not show that they penalise any agent who would ever make an exception.
A direct test would use cases in which the affected parties would plainly agree to the exception [24, 33].
text.formatted: A direct test would use cases in which the affected parties would plainly agree to the exception <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[24,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">33]</ref>.

text.text: Commitmentsignalling predicts that the Dogmatic agent should still be credited with the best character.
A contractualist account predicts that an agent who refuses an exception everyone would accept should lose that advantage.
In Studies 1 and 2, AI agents incurred a small additive shift toward systematic reasoning on character, significant within the moral domain only in the larger Study 2 sample (d = -0.15).
In Study 3 the Bayes factor strongly favoured no agent difference on character.
In Studies 1 and 2 the decision was left open, people expect AI to reason in more utilitarian ways [22], and Study 1 participants predicted that AI would reason systematically even on moral problems.
text.formatted: In Studies 1 and 2 the decision was left open, people expect AI to reason in more utilitarian ways <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[22]</ref>, and Study 1 participants predicted that AI would reason systematically even on moral problems.

text.text: The small AI penalty may therefore have reflected expectations about the AI's likely conclusions, which Study 3 controlled by fixing the decision.
Whether machines can have moral character is contestable, and many participants might deny it if asked directly.
Yet when asked which process better showed good character, they answered for an AI as they did for a person.
The dispositional reading above explains this.

The pairwise design shows that people apply the same inference to both agents, however, not that they credit an AI with as much character as a person, and we did not ask directly whether an AI can have character.
Agent type did matter for outcome judgements and thresholds.
Participants set a higher bar for an AI to deviate from a norm, and expected a dogmatic AI to produce better outcomes relative to a calibrated one than they did for a person.
People appear to want AI kept on rails for outcome reasons, without crediting it with better character for this.
Perceived competence did not explain it, since participants in the AI condition rated AI as more competent relative to people.
Another reason to limit an agent's discretion is doubt about its values.
Discretion is only as safe as the values that guide it, and a poorly aligned agent becomes more dangerous as its competence increases [34].
text.formatted: Discretion is only as safe as the values that guide it, and a poorly aligned agent becomes more dangerous as its competence increases <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">[34]</ref>.

text.text: If people are less sure of an AI's values than of a person's, they should want it held to rules whatever its competence.
We did not measure trust in the agent's values, so this remains open.
AI systems increasingly expose their reasoning through chain-of-thought traces, and there are good accountability reasons to favour such transparency [35].
text.formatted: AI systems increasingly expose their reasoning through chain-of-thought traces, and there are good accountability reasons to favour such transparency <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">[35]</ref>.

text.text: Our results suggest a specific risk in the moral domain.
Reasoning that visibly weighs whether to keep a norm, such as whether a lie would pay off in this case, may read as evidence that the norm is negotiable for the system.
The results do not imply that systems should hide their reasoning or reason less.
The cost in Study 3 attached to weighing the norm, not to effort.
A system can reason at length about how to apply a commitment, such as how to tell a painful truth with care, without reasoning about whether to keep it.
Whether people distinguish these two kinds of visible reasoning in practice is a question for future work.
First, Study 3 manipulated commitment, not intuition.
Its Dogmatic agent follows a rule, which may imply but does not entail intuition.

The link to Studies 1 and 2 rests on the observation that their systematic options weighed costs and benefits while their intuitive options did not, and we did not measure perceived negotiability in those studies.
A design that crosses intuitive and deliberative reasoning with the presence or absence of norm-weighing would test this directly.
Relatedly, the intuitive options in Studies 1 and 2 were framed in empathic terms.
Study 3 reduces this concern for the overall account but does not tell us how much of the earlier effects came from empathy.
Second, calibrated commitment was tested against one description of a threshold.
Participants judged the Calibrated agent much more negotiable than the Dogmatic agent, more so than the Act-weighing agent, so the escape clause may have read as more open than intended.
The three Negotiability contrasts were also far from additive (Dogmatic vs.
Act-weighing, M = -1.16, against a sum of -2.39 for the other two pairs), which suggests that participants rated each pair on the difference most salient within it.
The description also did not say whose gains could justify an exception.
A stronger test would vary the height of the threshold and who benefits from the exception separately.
Third, over half of all character ratings were at the scale maximum, which prevents a clean test of whether an unconditional commitment adds much beyond a calibrated one.
The data are consistent with a large step from no commitment to some commitment and a smaller premium for making it unconditional.
The comparative scales also measure only relative preferences.
A design in which each participant rates a single agent on absolute scales would remove the ceiling, show where each process falls, and test whether AI agents receive lower character ratings overall.
Fourth, all Study 3 scenarios described an agent holding a widely shared norm at modest cost, and the stated decision was the conventionally right one.
Commitment may be credited differently when the norm is contested or when holding it leads to a clearly worse outcome.
Finally, our samples were drawn from an online platform and skew Western and educated, and our AI was described, not interacted with.

People want different things from moral and non-moral decision-makers, preferring intuition in the moral domain and deliberation outside it, and they apply the same standard to artificial agents that they apply to each other.
They credit an AI with better moral character for reasoning intuitively about a moral problem even when told it cannot feel.
When the decision is held fixed, what they credit is the refusal to put the norm on the scale.

The preference for moral intuition, often explained by the warmth of genuine feeling, appears to be a preference for agents that do not treat moral norms as negotiable, and people are willing to attribute that to a machine.

Participants compared two of three processes (Dogmatic, Calibrated, Act-weighing) across seven scenarios in which an agent kept a widely shared moral norm, such as keeping a promise or not reading someone's private messages.

More generally, error-avoidance holds that character judgements follow expected outcomes, so it predicts no character-outcome gap.
Positive values favour the more committed process in each pair, which reverses the sign convention of Studies 1 and 2.

We set a target of 860 to allow for exclusions.
(H1) used a linear mixed model, Character ~ Agent × Pair + Scenario + (1 | Participant), with Satterthwaite p-values.

Scenario was a sum-coded fixed factor, so reported means average over the seven scenarios; with seven scenarios chosen to span distinct norms, we generalise across them informally through the scenario-level estimates rather than through a random effect.
The focal tests compared the estimated marginal mean of each pair against zero.

We computed d by dividing each estimate by the standard deviation of participant means over the seven scenarios, derived from the model's variance components, matching the definition used in the power analysis.
The character-outcome comparison (H2) tested whether commitment was credited more for character than for outcomes.
Each participant rated every scenario on both Moral Character and Best Outcome, so we combined the two ratings into one dataset with a variable coding which measure each rating came from.
We then fitted the same kind of model as for H1, adding Measure and its interactions with Agent and Pair.
The main effect of Measure gives the average gap, which the commitment accounts predict and error-avoidance does not.
The Measure × Pair and Measure × Agent interactions test whether the gap differs between process pairs or between agents.
The full model was Rating ~ Measure × Agent × Pair + Scenario + (1 + Measure | Participant).

The agent comparison (H3) was a 3-df likelihood-ratio test of the H1 model against the same model with all Agent terms removed, together with a Bayes factor for the no-Agent model computed on participant-mean Character scores (BayesFactor, default prior).
Exploratory analyses added Competence Comparison as a moderator of the H1 model and tested Agent effects on Commitment Threshold.
The remaining bipolar measures were analysed with the H1 model.
